newsitem.title: USA: Seminole Indians, U.S. governement sue over casinos.
newsitem.headline: Seminole Indians, U.S. governement sue over casinos.

text.p: The Seminole Tribe and the U.S. government have sued each other in a dispute over gambling operations at the Indian tribe's four casinos in Florida.
The tribe filed a suit against U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt on Friday in U.S. District Court in Fort Lauderdale.
The Seminoles alleged Babbitt failed to write rules that could allow full-fledged casino gambling on the reservations, as required by the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1988.

Tribal officials said in a statement they were forced to take legal action after U.S. Attorney Charles Wilson filed a suit in Tampa federal court earlier in the day asking a judge to order the tribe to remove more than 500 electronic slot machines he contends are illegal.
The tribe offers bingo, poker and video gaming machines at its casinos in Tampa, Immokalee, Brighton and Hollywood.

Wilson said federal law prohibited them from operating the slot machines and other casino-type or "Class III" games such as blackjack, roulette and craps, without a negoitated agreement with the state.
Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles has refused to sign an agreement permitting the reservations to offer those games, which are prohibited elsewhere in Florida.
Seminole Tribe Chairman James Billie said the tribe could offer full-fledged casino gaming if Babbitt issued rules and procedures authorizing it, regardless of the law in the surrounding state.

"It's too bad we have to sue the secretary to force him to do his job, but continued threats of litigation from the State of Florida and the Justice Department leave us little choice," Billie said in a statement.

The Seminoles sued Florida in federal court in 1991, seeking to force negotiations on casino gaming. But the federal courts ruled that the state had sovereign immunity from the lawsuit. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld the ruling.
Wilson said his lawsuit was not intended to shut down the Seminole casinos, "but to seek a declaratory judgment as to the legality of Class III gaming."

The Seminole tribe has about 2,500 members living on five reservations in Florida and received federal recognition as a sovereign nation in 1957. Many of the tribe's members are descendants of Seminoles who fled into the Florida Everglades to avoid deportation to the western states after the Indian wars in the 1800s.
